correctness.rationale: Every set of at least two vertices dominates a cocktail party graph because an outside vertex has only one nonneighbor, so an MDRDF has at most one zero. If there is no zero, weight at most 2n+1 leaves at most one label-two vertex and no label three; its partner is an undefended label-one vertex. With one zero, the baseline on positive vertices is 2n-1 and the zero requires two excess units. At equality, one label three fails because its partner is a label-one vertex with no high-labeled neighbor. Therefore exactly two label-two vertices occur, both adjacent to the zero. Conversely every such placement is feasible, proving the value, complete classification, and count. The independent checker exhausts all labelings for n=2..5.

value.rationale: Cocktail party graphs are a standard symmetric family and the complement of a perfect matching, making them a natural dense benchmark for domination variants. The theorem gives a complete equality classification rather than a routine scalar substitution. It isolates a distinctive interaction between maximality and the unique-nonneighbor structure, and the exact optimizer count is reusable enumerative information.
